title: Policy optimization can be memory-efficient: LLM Alignment Through Successive Policy Re-weighting (SPR)

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to reduce the compute/memory cost of RL-based policy optimization for LLM alignment to the level of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while still leveraging an explicit reward model and online data. This specific objective — achieving RLHF-level alignment efficiency at SFT-level resource costs — is not directly addressed in any prior paper. While many papers (e.g., [1], [7], [9], [15]) discuss RLHF and its computational challenges, none explicitly aim to match SFT's resource efficiency while retaining RLHF's core elements (reward model, online data). Papers like [8] (ORPO) and [11] (DPO) explore alternative approaches to preference optimization but do not target the same compute/memory reduction goal relative to SFT.

**VERDICT purpose = NONE**

---

### Mechanism
The mechanism, Successive Policy Re-weighting (SPR), reformulates the TRPO/PPO objective as a constrained optimization problem solved via successive minimization. It alternates between fitting a Q-value function and a log-sum-exp reference function, then updates the policy using a supervised re-weighting loss. This mechanism is partially covered by prior work. Papers like [5] (SPU) and [6] (AWR) use supervised learning to update policies in reinforcement learning, and [13] (RCPO) employs alternating optimization for constrained policy updates. However, none of these papers combine these elements in the specific SPR formulation, which integrates Q-value fitting, log-sum-exp reference functions, and supervised re-weighting. The sentence-level simplification (horizon=1) is also not explicitly present in prior work.

**VERDICT mechanism = NONE**

---

### Evaluation
The evaluation design estimates memory usage (e.g., Pythia-1B, TL;DR, batch 2, single device) and compares SPR against SFT, PPO, and DPO. This type of evaluation — measuring memory usage across different RLHF and preference optimization methods — is covered by prior work. For example, [15] (ReaL) evaluates RLHF training efficiency, including memory and compute costs, and [8] (ORPO) compares memory usage across preference optimization methods. While the specific benchmarks and models differ, the evaluation design (memory comparison across methods) is not novel.

**VERDICT evaluation = 15**

---

### Domain
The domain is LLM alignment via reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). This domain is extensively covered by prior work, including [1], [7], [9], and [15], all of which focus on RLHF for aligning LLMs with human preferences.

**VERDICT domain = 1**  

---

---

**PURPOSE: Reduce compute/memory cost of RL-based policy optimization for LLM alignment to SFT level, while retaining explicit reward model and online data.**

Paper [15] (ReaL) addresses efficient RLHF training of LLMs and explicitly discusses the high compute/memory cost of RLHF (multiple model instances), proposing parameter reallocation to reduce overhead. However, its goal is efficient scheduling/parallelization, not reducing to SFT-level memory by reformulating the optimization. Paper [7] discusses PPO secrets for LLMs but doesn't target SFT-level memory reduction. Paper [8] (ORPO) eliminates the reference model to reduce cost but abandons the explicit reward model and online RL. Paper [16] discusses on-policy vs. off-policy preference fine-tuning but doesn't target SFT-level memory. No prior paper specifically targets "reduce RLHF memory to SFT level while keeping explicit reward model and online data" — the closest is [15] which targets efficiency but via a different mechanism and without the SFT-equivalence goal. The purpose is genuinely distinct from all prior papers.

---

**MECHANISM: Successive Policy Re-weighting (SPR) — reformulate TRPO/PPO as constrained optimization solved by successive minimization alternating between Q-value fitting and log-sum-exp reference (value) function fitting, then policy update via supervised re-weighting (increase/decrease log-likelihood by advantage Q-W); only one model loaded per step.**

Paper [5] (SPU — Supervised Policy Update) is highly relevant: "SPU formulates and solves a constrained optimization problem in the non-parameterized proximal policy space. Using supervised regression, it then converts the optimal non-parameterized policy to a parameterized policy." This is essentially the same primitive: reformulate the TRPO/PPO constrained optimization, solve it in a non-parametric space, then fit the policy via supervised regression. The alternating/successive structure and the re-weighting of log-likelihoods by advantages is also present in Paper [6] (AWR — Advantage-Weighted Regression): "two standard supervised learning steps: one to regress onto target values for a value function, and another to regress onto advantage-weighted returns for the policy." AWR explicitly fits a value function then updates policy via advantage-weighted log-likelihood, which is the same primitive as SPR's Q-W advantage re-weighting. Paper [18] (REPS) also uses relative entropy constraints and closed-form re-weighting solutions. The core mechanism — alternating between fitting a value/Q function and updating policy via supervised advantage-weighted regression — is covered by [5] and [6].

---

**EVALUATION: Estimated peak memory comparison (SPR ≈ SFT < DPO < PPO) on Pythia-1B, TL;DR, batch 2, single device.**

No prior paper uses this specific evaluation design of comparing peak GPU memory across RLHF methods (PPO, DPO, SFT, SPR) on a fixed model/dataset/batch configuration. Paper [15] discusses memory/compute efficiency of RLHF but uses throughput and training time metrics, not a peak memory comparison against SFT as baseline. Paper [24] (QLoRA) discusses memory reduction for fine-tuning but in a quantization context. The evaluation design here — a memory footprint comparison across alignment methods benchmarked against SFT as the target — does not appear in any prior paper as a named benchmark, metric family, or established protocol. This is a newly constructed comparison metric/protocol specific to this contribution.

**DOMAIN: LLM alignment / reinforcement learning from human feedback.**

Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [7], [8], [9], [14], [15], [16] all operate in LLM alignment / RLHF. This domain is thoroughly covered.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to empirically verify that SPR aligns LLMs at least as well as memory-heavier baselines while leveraging offline+online data. Paper [2] discusses offline alignment methods for LLMs using RLHF and preference optimization, which overlaps with the general goal of aligning LLMs with human preferences. Paper [7] also addresses iterative preference optimization for LLM alignment, specifically comparing DPO and iterative methods, which is substantively equivalent to the purpose of the contribution. Paper [17] introduces self-play-based preference optimization for LLM alignment, which similarly aims to improve alignment using offline and iterative methods. These papers share the same problem-class level objective of aligning LLMs with human preferences using offline and iterative approaches.

### Mechanism
The contribution's mechanism involves comparing SPR against PPO, DPO, and Best-of-N sampling on specific models and tasks. Paper [7] introduces iterative length-regularized DPO, which is a direct iterative preference optimization method. Paper [8] discusses Best-of-N sampling for LLM alignment and its relationship to DPO and RLHF, which is substantively equivalent to the mechanism of comparing SPR against Best-of-N and DPO. Paper [11] introduces statistical rejection sampling for preference optimization, which is conceptually similar to SPR's iterative sampling approach. Paper [17] proposes self-play-based preference optimization, which is another iterative alignment mechanism. These papers collectively cover the mechanism at the primitive level.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves comparing SPR and baselines (DPO, PPO, Best-of-N) on TL;DR summarization (using a reward model and GPT-3.5 for win rate evaluation) and OpenLLM leaderboard benchmarks. Paper [7] uses iterative DPO with online preferences and evaluates alignment improvements on reasoning tasks, which is substantively equivalent to the evaluation design of iterative preference optimization on benchmarks. Paper [8] evaluates Best-of-N sampling on alignment tasks, which matches the evaluation design of comparing sampling-based methods. Paper [10] conducts a comprehensive study comparing DPO and PPO for LLM alignment, which aligns with the evaluation design of comparing preference optimization methods. Paper [11] evaluates statistical rejection sampling for preference optimization, which involves similar benchmark-based validation. These papers collectively cover the evaluation design.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM alignment, specifically targeting text summarization and reasoning benchmarks. Paper [1] explicitly identifies LLM alignment as an active research area, covering the general domain. Paper [7] focuses on iterative preference optimization for instruction tuning and reasoning tasks, which falls within the same domain. Paper [8] addresses alignment using Best-of-N sampling, which is also part of the LLM alignment domain. Paper [17] discusses self-play-based preference optimization for LLM alignment, further covering the domain. These papers collectively address the same application area of LLM alignment.

**PURPOSE: Empirically verify that SPR aligns LLMs at least as well as memory-heavier baselines while leveraging offline+online data.**

The purpose is to demonstrate that a specific alignment method (SPR) matches or beats PPO/DPO/Best-of-N while being more memory-efficient, using both offline and online data. Paper [10] "Is DPO Superior to PPO for LLM Alignment? A Comprehensive Study" directly compares reward-based (PPO) vs reward-free (DPO) methods for LLM alignment empirically. Paper [11] "Statistical Rejection Sampling Improves Preference Optimization" compares offline methods (SLiC, DPO) against online RL (PPO) and shows competitive performance. Paper [15] "TSO: Self-Training with Scaled Preference Optimization" also empirically compares alignment methods including DPO variants with iterative/online approaches. However, the specific purpose of showing a *memory-efficient* method using offline+online data that matches heavier baselines is most closely matched by [10] and [11], which both empirically compare PPO, DPO, and related methods for LLM alignment — same objective at the problem-class level.

**MECHANISM: Compare SPR against PPO, DPO, and Best-of-N on a 1B model (Pythia-1B on TL;DR summarization) and an 8B model (LLaMA3-SFT, OpenLLM leaderboard).**

The mechanism is a comparative evaluation of alignment algorithms (PPO, DPO, Best-of-N) on specific model sizes and benchmarks. Paper [10] explicitly compares PPO vs DPO comprehensively on LLM alignment tasks. Paper [11] compares PPO, DPO, SLiC on TL;DR summarization with Pythia models and reward model evaluation — this is strikingly similar. Paper [8] "BoNBoN Alignment" compares Best-of-N against RLHF/DPO approaches. The combination of comparing these exact methods (PPO, DPO, Best-of-N) appears across [10], [11], and [8].

**EVALUATION: TL;DR summarization with reward model scoring + GPT-judged win rate; OpenLLM leaderboard benchmarks including GSM8K.**

Paper [11] uses TL;DR summarization with Pythia models and reward model evaluation — same benchmark family and metric semantics. Paper [10] uses similar reward model + win rate evaluation designs for LLM alignment. Paper [7] uses iterative DPO with OpenLLM leaderboard evaluation. The evaluation design (reward score + GPT win rate on TL;DR, OpenLLM leaderboard) is covered by [11] (TL;DR + reward model) and [7] (OpenLLM leaderboard).

Multiple papers work in LLM alignment: [1], [2], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [13], [15], [17], [19], [20] all operate in LLM alignment. This domain is clearly covered.
